issues.legal_issue: A repeal-and-re-enactment provision that comprehensively specifies the effect of repeal may exclude the general savings rule.
material_facts: The legislation governing the pending confirmation application was successively repealed and replaced.
The successor legislation expressly addressed the previous operation of the repealed law and deemed actions taken under it to have been taken under the successor legislation.
issues.conclusion: The general savings provision did not apply because the successor legislation contained a self-contained provision indicating an intention to exclude it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, ordinarily applies to repeal followed by fresh legislation unless the new legislation manifests a contrary intention. Applying State of Punjab v. Mohar Singh, the Court held that section 58(3) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, was self-contained: it addressed the effect of repeal in terms that excluded section 6.

predicates.repeal_and_reenactment_case: A proceeding arose under a law that was repealed and replaced by successor legislation.
predicates.successor_law_comprehensively_specifies_: The successor legislation itself specified how repeal affects prior operations and actions taken under the earlier law.

issues.definition: When a proceeding involves repeal and reenactment and the successor law comprehensively specifies the effect of repeal, the general savings rule is excluded.

issues.legal_issue: A right to have a pending application determined with the benefit of finality does not vest before the determination is made.
material_facts: An application for confirmation was filed under the earlier law and remained pending when later legislation came into force.
No confirmation order had been made before the earlier law was replaced.
The confirmation order was made after the successor legislation had taken effect.
issues.conclusion: The applicant had no vested right, upon filing the application, to a determination carrying the finality provided by the earlier law.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 5-B of the East Punjab Evacuees’ (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, finality attached when an order was made. The Court distinguished Colonial Sugar Refining Co. Ltd. v. Irving, which concerned a right of appeal in a pending action, and Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd. v. Income-Tax Commissioner, where final orders already existed. A right to finality, if it exists, arises only when the determination is actually made.

predicates.pending_statutory_application: A person filed an application under a statute that remained undecided.
predicates.no_determination_before_law_change: The statute changed before any decision was made on the application.

issues.definition: When a statutory application remains pending through a change in law and no determination has yet been made, the applicant has no vested right to finality under the former law.

issues.legal_issue: A pending application governed by successor legislation is to be decided under that legislation, and an order made under it is subject to its revisional powers.
material_facts: The application for confirmation was pending when the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, came into force.
The confirmation order was made after that Act had come into force.
The successor legislation provided for revision of orders made by a Custodian.
issues.conclusion: The pending application had to be decided under the successor legislation, and the order made on it was subject to the Custodian-General’s revisional power.
issues.legal_principle: Section 58(3) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, preserves the previous operation of the repealed law and deems actions taken under it to have been taken under the new law. The scheme is that matters to which the new Act applies are dealt with under that Act, except for consequences already ensued or acts already completed. Section 27 conferred revisional power on the Custodian-General.

predicates.evacuee_property_confirmation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an application to confirm a transaction involving evacuee property.
predicates.application_pending_at_law_change: The confirmation application remained undecided when the governing law changed.
predicates.decision_made_under_successor_law: The authority decided the pending application after the successor law had taken effect.

issues.definition: When an evacuee-property confirmation application is pending at a change in law and is decided afterward, the decision is subject to the successor law’s revisional powers.

issues.legal_issue: A broadly conferred revisional power to examine legality or propriety is not barred merely because an appeal was available but not pursued.
material_facts: A Custodian made an original order on a confirmation application.
The governing legislation empowered the Custodian-General to examine the legality or propriety of a Custodian’s order in revision.
An appeal was available, but no appeal was filed.
issues.conclusion: The Custodian-General’s revisional power was not precluded by the availability of an appeal that had not been filed, and it was not confined to jurisdictional or legal errors.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, authorized the Custodian-General to call for the record of a proceeding in which a Custodian had passed an order and to act to satisfy himself as to its legality or propriety. The Court held that the provision’s terms did not support the proposed limitations.

predicates.revision_of_custodian_order: The proceeding is a revision seeking review of an order made by a Custodian.
predicates.revision_power_covers_legality_or_propri: The applicable revisional power authorizes review of the order’s legality or propriety.
predicates.appeal_available_but_not_filed: A person could have appealed the order, but no appeal was filed.

issues.definition: When a Custodian’s order is under revision under a power covering legality or propriety, the revision is not barred or narrowed merely because an available appeal was not filed.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional decision that leaves the scope of remand unclear and may constrain reconsideration should be set aside for fresh consideration.
material_facts: The Supreme Court was hearing an appeal against the Custodian-General’s revisional decision.
The decision set aside a confirmation order and remitted the matter, but it was unclear whether the remand was general or limited.
The Custodian-General had made findings and expressed views that could make it difficult for the authority reconsidering the matter to address the issues afresh.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the revisional decision and remitted the matter to the Custodian-General for fresh consideration, with an opportunity for both sides to present their views and clarification of any further remand.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising its appellate jurisdiction, the Court held that the unclear scope and reasoning of the revisional decision made it difficult to maintain. It directed fresh consideration and stated that, if the matter were remanded again, the matters to be considered should be clearly indicated. The Court expressed no opinion on the disputed merits of the confirmation.

predicates.appeal_against_revisional_decision: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an authority’s revisional decision.
predicates.remand_scope_unclear: The revisional decision does not make clear whether its remand is general or limited.
predicates.findings_may_constrain_reconsideration: The decision includes findings or views that may prevent the matter from being reconsidered openly.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a revisional decision whose remand scope is unclear and whose findings may constrain reconsideration, the decision is set aside for fresh consideration.
